title: Jude and the Deadline
premise: Rosalind Thackeray, a burned-out interpreter for a collapsing peace delegation, receives a calendar invitation from her handler, Marcus Vane—sent hours after his body was pulled from the harbor. The invitation leads her to a dead-drop containing proof that the peace talks were engineered to fail, with three governments complicit and a professional assassin, only known as the Chorister, erasing everyone who knew. Hunted by the assassin, disavowed by her own delegation, and running low on allies, Rosalind races to move the evidence to a journalist and an honest prosecutor before the 6 a.m. extraction flight. At the airfield she trades herself to the Chorister for the evidence's safe delivery, survives by turning the assassin's own handler against him, and boards the flight as dawn breaks—alive, exposed, and finally able to sleep.
about_author: Ada Whitlock is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent a decade in rooms where what wasn't said mattered more than what was. She writes thrillers about people whose professions force them to be invisible.

chapters.title: Invitation from the Dead
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Three weeks after Marcus Vane's drowning, her phone buzzes: a meeting invitation from his account, tomorrow, 11 p.m., the old customs house. She almost deletes it. The emotional beat is dread sharpening into a terrible, welcome purpose—insomnia finally has a destination.

chapters.title: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She goes, against every instinct, and finds a dead-drop: a burner phone, a keycard, and a note in Vane's shorthand—only she can read it. Someone watches her from across the square. Beat: fear fused with the first proof she isn't crazy.

chapters.title: Delegation of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Back at the peace summit, she interprets a negotiation she now suspects is theater. Her new handler, Aldous Brand, is too smooth, too curious about her night. Beat: the claustrophobia of performing normalcy while the room itself feels staged.

chapters.title: What Vane Knew
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV, with a flashback to Vane. The keycard opens a storage unit: recordings Vane made of back-channel meetings—evidence the talks were designed to collapse, justifying intervention. Beat: vertigo; the incident that broke her sleep is tangled in this.

chapters.title: The Chorister
chapters.summary: Assassin's POV, unnamed. He reviews a kill list; Vane's death was his work, and the invitation was sent before Vane died—a loose thread. He identifies Rosalind as a target but delays, curious why Vane trusted her. Beat: cold professionalism with a hairline crack of intrigue.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Lie
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She deciphers the recordings: each delegation's leadership signed off on failure. She tries to reach Vane's listed contact, a journalist named Okafor, and finds his office tossed. Beat: the price of knowledge—the world she trusted shrinks to a storage unit's worth of proof.

chapters.title: Brand's Offer
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Handler Aldous Brand corners her: he knows she took something. He offers protection in exchange for the recordings, claiming he's a whistleblower inside the machine. Beat: seductive relief curdling into doubt—his story is one detail too polished.

chapters.title: The Incident, Replayed
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. A recording reveals the truth of the incident that haunts her: a massacre at a checkpoint that the delegations buried, and that her interpretation was edited to conceal. Vane kept the unedited tape because of her. Beat: grief and fury; her guilt was manufactured.

chapters.title: Safe House, Unsafe
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She hides with a low-level delegation driver, Tomas, who asks no questions. The Chorister finds them anyway; Tomas is wounded covering her escape. Beat: the cost of proximity—belonging has a body count, and she keeps the ledger.

chapters.title: Okafor
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She reaches journalist Ifeoma Okafor through a dead-letter protocol Vane taught her. Okafor confirms the pattern: three sources, all dead, all interpreters. Beat: solidarity at last—two keepers of other people's words, deciding to publish their own.

chapters.title: Deadline Set
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. The delegation announces early withdrawal; the extraction flight leaves at dawn, and everyone on it will be beyond subpoena. Okafor needs 12 hours to verify; the Chorister is closing in. Beat: the clock becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: Brand's True Face
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Brand's protection was a trap to recover and destroy the tapes; she escapes his safe house with only the checkpoint recording, the rest seized. Beat: betrayal—she almost handed the truth to the machine that built the lie.

chapters.title: The Chorister's Handler
chapters.summary: Assassin's POV. His own controller orders him to kill Rosalind and burn the evidence, but the controller's name appears in Vane's tapes as an architect of the checkpoint massacre. Beat: the professional discovers his employers are the criminals.

chapters.title: Bargaining in the Dark
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She contacts the Chorister directly through Vane's burner, offering him the tape that damns his handler in exchange for passage to the airfield. Beat: terror braided with audacity—she negotiates with the man sent to erase her.

chapters.title: What the Interpreter Heard
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. She makes a copy of the checkpoint tape and records her own sworn account, naming names, in three languages. Beat: reclaiming her voice—the woman paid to translate lies testifies in her own words.

chapters.title: The Handoff
chapters.summary: Rosalind and the Chorister, alternating POV. The exchange in a rail yard goes wrong: Brand's men intervene, the tape scatters, and the Chorister takes a bullet shielding the copy—his handler's order now aimed at him. Beat: uneasy alliance forged under fire.

chapters.title: Okafor's Twelve Hours
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. Racing verification with two prosecutors in two countries, she publishes a partial leak to freeze the story before the flight can spirit witnesses away. Beat: the machinery of lawful justice grinding, too slow and just fast enough.

chapters.title: Airfield at Night
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. The delegation's convoy reaches the airfield; Brand tries to put her on the plane as a silenced witness. She refuses, walks toward the lights, and the Chorister appears at her side—not as her killer, but as her witness against his handler. Beat: the point of no return.

chapters.title: Confrontation on the Tarmac
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Brand, exposed by the leak, attempts a final erasure; the Chorister turns his gun on his own chain of command while Rosalind, microphone from the press pool in hand, forces Brand to repeat his orders on record. Beat: climax—truth spoken aloud, at gunpoint, in three languages.

chapters.title: Dawn Flight
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. The plane leaves without her. She chooses to stay and face prosecutors rather than vanish—justice outside the law got her here; justice inside it must finish the work. Beat: surrender as strength.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. Weeks later, she testifies at the inquiry; the checkpoint massacre is acknowledged, Brand and two ministers are indicted, the Chorister disappears into a deal no one discusses. Beat: imperfect justice, honestly bought.

chapters.title: The First Night
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV. In a small rented flat, she sleeps through the night for the first time since the incident, Vane's shorthand notebook on the nightstand. Beat: resolution—belonging, she learns, begins with refusing to be invisible to yourself.
